11135-monarch-the-big-bear-of-tallac:
Ernest Thompson Seton published this 1919 animal biography, Monarch, the Big Bear of Tallac, with one hundred drawings. Seton dedicates the book to the memory of days in Tallac's pines, where by the fire he heard the epic tale from two rough men of the hills, leader and led.

Their tale is a parable of hill-born power that fades when it finds the plains, like a giant redwood grown from a tiny seed, an avalanche born a snowflake. Chapters follow two springs, the trout pool, the stream that sank in the sand, and fire and water. In one scene, bear and man share a pool while flames rage, each keeping nose and eye above water.
1330-the-story-of-little-black-sambo-and:
Made up by Helen Bannerman for her own small daughters in India, these two short picture tales were first told on a long train ride. In the first, a small boy sets out in fine new clothes and meets one tiger after another, giving up a coat, trousers, shoes, and umbrella to escape being eaten.

Each tiger then claims to be the grandest in the jungle, and their quarrel round a palm tree melts them into butter for his mother's pancakes. The second tale follows an orphan girl named Mingo, sent to fetch river water by a cross old guardian. A mugger breaks her water pot, and her errands grow worse from there. Both are simple adventures built for reading aloud to very young children.
14090-elements-of-debating-a-manual-for-:
Leverett S. Lyon wrote this 1919 manual for high-school and academy students learning to argue in public. Ten lessons move from the nature of argument to the shape of a debate: finding the issues, choosing evidence, building a brief, and handling refutation. Appendices add sample analyses, a model college forensic, and lists of debatable questions for classroom use.

Practice matters more than theory here. Lyon treats refutation as the heart of debate, since a speaker must both build a case and pull down the other side's proof. Later lessons cover timekeeping, team roles, and judging forms. A long example on city commission government shows students how facts about Galveston, Houston, and Des Moines can support a claim about economy. Teachers still recognize the method: clear issues, honest evidence, and answers ready before the other side speaks.
15896-five-months-at-anzac:
A war narrative by Colonel Joseph Lievesley Beeston, officer commanding the Fourth Field Ambulance, Australian Imperial Force. Angus and Robertson issued it in Sydney in 1916, with photographs, including Anzac Cove by Lieutenant-Colonel Millard. Beeston dedicates the book to his ambulance officers, non-commissioned officers, and men. Five months at Gallipoli fill its pages.

Beeston tells of landing, dressing stations, and the daily work of saving wounded men under fire. His ambulance served the New Zealand and Australian Division. The tone stays plain and loyal, praising devotion to duty without fine words. The narrative stands as a medical history of Anzac: courage measured in stretchers, bandages, and steadfast hands.
20488-henry-of-monmouth-volume-1-or-memo:
Henry of Monmouth is a biography of the prince who became King Henry V of England. This first volume covers his life and character before the crown. The dedication addresses a reigning queen in loyal terms, wishing her a long and peaceful reign.

The writer prays that the queen may enjoy the favor of the Spirit of Truth. After wearing her diadem in honor among a happy people, she may exchange it for a better crown. The volume then follows the young prince through the wars and court struggles that trained the future victor of Agincourt.
20489-henry-of-monmouth-volume-2-or-memo:
The second volume of Henry of Monmouth takes up the life of Henry V from his accession. His father, Henry IV, died at Westminster on Monday, March 20, 1413. The new king's proclamation bore date the very next day, March 21.

Never, the biographer writes, was any prince's coming to a throne hailed with more general joy. The volume follows Henry's reign: his claims in France, his campaigns, and the fame that Shakespeare later fixed in the public mind. It closes the two-volume memoir of the most celebrated soldier king of medieval England.
22005-how-to-add-ten-years-to-your-life-:
S. S. Curry ran the Boston School of Expression, and he set out his rules for a longer, fuller life in a book printed in 1915. Its full title promises ten added years and twice the satisfaction. Curry opens with the poet Bryant, who said a simple morning exercise had lengthened his life. The claim sets the tone: small habits, kept daily, change the whole body.

Curry urges readers to wake gladly, breathe deep, stretch, and meet the day without fear. Voice, posture, and cheerfulness all count as health habits in his scheme. The advice is plain and hopeful rather than medical. Modern readers may smile at its faith, but the core counsel, move and breathe and begin early, still sounds familiar.
23321-the-choctaw-freedmen-and-the-story:
This history tells of the Choctaw freedmen and the Oak Hill Industrial Academy, a school for freedpeople in Indian Territory. An oak tree on a slope near the academy serves as emblem: strong, stalwart, and useful, like an intelligent and noble man.

Portraits such as Alice Lee Elliott anchor a story of schooling, work, and uplift after slavery. The book preserves the academy's record and the freedmen's own struggle for learning, and it remains a valuable source for Black and Native history in Oklahoma. The academy record preserves freedmen's struggle for learning after slavery. At Oak Hill, family worship brought students and teachers together for daily Scripture reading and prayer.
24612-the-monitor-and-the-merrimac:
Lieutenant J. L. Worden and Lieutenant S. D. Greene of the Monitor, with H. Ashton Ramsay, chief engineer of the Merrimac, tell both sides of the famous ironclad duel of 9 March 1862. Harper and Brothers published their accounts at New York and London in 1912, with illustrations including the encounter at short range.

Worden and Greene describe the Monitor's fight from the Union turret, while Ramsay gives the Confederate view from the Merrimac's engine room. Together they show the first battle between ironclad warships, as the men who fought it saw it. Readers of naval history will find this short book a classic of firsthand testimony.
26690-the-pirates-of-panama-or-the-bucca:
John Esquemeling, one of the buccaneers present at the deeds he describes, wrote this true account of Sir Henry Morgan and other freebooters of the Spanish Main. George Alfred Williams edited and illustrated it for Frederick A. Stokes at New York in 1914. Esquemeling sailed for the western islands in French West India Company service, met an English frigate, reached Tortuga, and was twice sold there.

Chapters describe Tortuga and Hispaniola, the French buccaneers, Pierre le Grand, and Francis Lolonois, before Morgan takes center stage. Morgan seizes Puerto Bello and Maracaibo, takes St. Catherine's and the castle of Chagre, then marches twelve hundred men to take Panama. It is an eyewitness pirate history, bloody, detailed, and proud of its outlaws.
28958-the-road-to-frontenac:
Samuel Merwin wrote this 1901 historical novel, The Road to Frontenac, published by Doubleday, Page in New York. Captain Daniel Menard leans on a citadel balcony in clear, still air, and the story that follows carries him through New France and Indian country. Chapters bring the maid, the long arrow, Danton breaking out, and the fight at La Gallette, with a night council and the voice of the great mountain.

Later chapters move to the long house, where the dead sit, the bad doctor, and the long lake, northward to Frontenac itself. A frontispiece shows Indians chained two and two down steps. Readers get a stirring adventure of French Canada and the Iroquois frontier, told with period color and a soldier's pace.
29135-with-the-night-mail-a-story-of-200:
Rudyard Kipling wrote this story of the year 2000, published with extracts from the contemporary magazine in which it appeared. Kipling imagines a world where night mail travels by air, with scheduled aerial routes, ports, and the working routines of a future postal service. The tale reads like a logbook crossed with a magazine report.

Kipling's future is orderly and technical, full of craft, weather, and timetables, rather than wonders for their own sake. The added magazine extracts let readers see how the story first reached its audience. Readers get a founding work of air-age science fiction, practical in imagination and confident about a coming age of flight.
29473-blood-and-iron-origin-of-german-em:
John Hubert Greusel's 1915 book, printed by the Shakespeare Press of New York, traces the origin of the German Empire as revealed by the character of its founder, Bismarck. Its first book treats Bismarck's human essence: the giant's ponderous hammer, a genius combined with foibles, and a rise to power rooted in iron-headed ancestry. Later chapters fight fire with fire, find a voice in the wilderness, and watch the young giant bellow defiance.

Greusel writes as a character study, not a dry chronicle, seeking the man inside the statesman. The book's wartime date colors its portrait. Readers of German history will find a vivid, partisan life of Bismarck that reads his empire through his temper and will.
30258-the-fighting-governor-a-chronicle-:
Charles W. Colby chronicles Frontenac, the fighting governor, in a Toronto and Glasgow volume from 1915. Canada in 1672 opens, followed by Louis de Buade, Comte de Frontenac, his first years in Canada, and the triangle of governor, bishop, and intendant. Frontenac's public policy, a lurid interval, the great struggle, and his last days complete the narrative, with a bibliographical note and index.

A colour drawing by C. W. Jefferys fronts the book, showing Frontenac answering Phips's messenger in 1690. Other pictures show Lady Frontenac from Versailles, Jean Baptiste Colbert, and Robert Cavelier de La Salle. Colby writes popular history in the Brook chronicle manner, brisk and clear, for readers who want New France under a bold, quarrelsome governor.
30607-australia-its-history-and-present-:
Rev. W. Pridden writes Australia, Its History and Present Condition, containing an account both of the bush and of the colonies, with their respective inhabitants, in the Englishman's Library series, number twenty-six. Pridden, vicar of Broxbourne, presents a mid-Victorian survey of a growing continent.

Transcriber notes keep original spellings such as Morrumbidgee and Murrumbidgee, civilisation and civilization, and colonisation and colonization, each used on several occasions. The book covers bush life, colonies, settlers, and Indigenous inhabitants, aiming at a readable history and present condition for English readers. It serves as a period view of Australia in formation. The style is plain and direct. It moves from town to bush, from port to farm, and from past to present, so a new reader can follow the land and its people.
31453-the-southern-soldier-boy-a-thousan:
James Carson Elliott's The Southern Soldier Boy is subtitled A Thousand Shots for the Confederacy. It is the memoir of a soldier of Company F, 56th Regiment, North Carolina Troops, Confederate States Army, from 1861 to 1865, written from Shelby, North Carolina. Elliott presents historical incidents, reminiscences, and personal experiences, covering the nine months' siege of Petersburg and both prison pens, as the title page states.

The memoir gives the Confederate private's view of the war's last years: camp life, battle, capture, and imprisonment. Elliott writes plainly, as a veteran recalling what he saw, rather than as a historian arguing a case. For readers of Civil War memoirs, the book is a valuable firsthand account from the ranks, with the detail and directness that only a participant could supply.
3164-women-in-the-life-of-balzac:
Juanita H Floyd studies the women around Honoré de Balzac in this volume, number ninety-six in a series by or about the French novelist. Balzac's life was crowded with mothers, sisters, patrons, lovers, and readers, and Floyd sorts their roles in shaping the man and his work. The book treats biography as a way into the novels, not as gossip beside them.

Madame Hanska, the countess Balzac pursued for years and at last married, stands at the center of the later story. Earlier figures, from his mother to his first patrons, fill the first chapters. Scholarly care, without romantic varnish, gives Balzac's circle its human shape.
3625-honore-de-balzac:
Albert Keim and Louis Lumet write a life of Honore de Balzac, translated from the French by Frederic Taber Cooper and published in 1914. The book belongs to a series on great lives meant to train mind and character by example, teaching effort, devotion, industry, heroism, and sacrifice. Chapters follow Balzac from a treatise on the human will and a Paris garret through apprenticeship, business failure, first success, and dandyism.

Later chapters treat the foreign lady who became his wife and his vast fictional world, the Human Comedy. Keim and Lumet write with admiration for Balzac's energy and his eye for money, class, and desire. The life suits readers new to Balzac who want a clear path into his novels.
3712-the-chateau-of-prince-polignac:
Anthony Trollope takes readers to Le Puy, a town in south central France built among abrupt volcanic rocks, for this tale of travel and courtship. An English lady on tour lodges near the old chateau of Prince Polignac and weighs the charms of the place against the puzzle of a new acquaintance, a courteous Frenchman named Lacordaire. She knows nothing of his income or trade, and her maid can only report that he is a merchant.

The comedy lies in that gap between romance and prudence, as the lady argues with herself about respect, kindness, and safety in a match. Volcanic crags, narrow valleys, and old stone give the story a vivid backdrop. It is a quiet tale, best for readers who enjoy manners, place, and the slow work of making up one's mind.
3822-balzac:
Frederick Lawton wrote this life of Honore de Balzac to show that the novelist's life explains his books. Lawton opens against a critic who doubted biography could matter, answering that Balzac's novels literally are his life, full of the same debts, schemes, and furious work. The sculptor Rodin's statue of Balzac first tempted Lawton to write, and the dedication honors Rodin's synthetic portraiture.

The middle chapters show Balzac writing at high pressure, selling The Old Maid for eight thousand francs after three nights' work and dashing off Facino Cane in a single night. Rossini, meeting him mid spell, hears that Balzac sees only the coffin as rest, yet calls work a fine shroud. Readers who love the Human Comedy will find its author here, tireless and forever in debt.
443-the-love-affairs-of-a-bibliomaniac:
Eugene Field celebrates book collecting in this set of sketches, introduced by his brother after Field's death. Field, a Chicago journalist for a quarter century, hunted rare books at great personal cost while mocking fellow collectors in print. His prayer of the bibliomaniac begs to be beset by temptation in bookshops.

Sketches follow auctions, stalls, and prized finds, with humor for the half-pathetic, half-comic lure of old books. Field knew the disease from inside and loved it still. The book charms all who have ever paid too much for a volume they could not leave behind.
5146-the-fighting-governor-a-chronicle-o:
Charles W. Colby's chronicle, volume seven of the Chronicles of Canada, tells the story of Louis de Buade, Comte de Frontenac, governor of New France. Chapters follow Canada in 1672, Frontenac's first years, his quarrels with bishop and intendant, his public policy, and the great struggle with the English colonies that filled his later rule.

Colby writes a compact, readable history for general readers, drawing on the records of a colony of fewer than seven thousand people when Frontenac arrived. The book offers a clear introduction to French Canada's most famous governor and to the wars and politics that shaped North America.
7009-monsieur-de-pourceaugnac:
Moliere's Monsieur de Pourceaugnac, acted on October 6, 1669, appears here in Charles Heron Wall's English prose, with short introductions and notes. Wall calls it nothing but a farce, yet holds Moliere excels in farce as in higher comedy, and ranks this among his best. The attacks on the doctors of the time are not exaggerated, he adds, and Moliere himself played the title part.

The cast sets Pourceaugnac against Oronte, father of Julia, and Eraste, her lover, with Sbrigani the Neapolitan adventurer stirring plots. Two physicians, an apothecary, peasants, Swiss guards, police, and the intriguing Nerine and Lucette fill the Paris scene. The farce turns on a provincial gentleman mocked, doctored, and married off by wits.
8598-introduction-to-the-dramas-of-balza:
Epiphanius Wilson and J. Walker McSpadden introduce Honore de Balzac as a dramatist, a side of the novelist most readers miss. Wilson's essay argues that Balzac is known to the world as the author of the Comedie Humaine. The great series describing French society from the Revolution to the Restoration. He analyses manners, motives, and daily life across every class. The dramas, Wilson suggests, carry the same ambition onto the stage.

McSpadden's companion piece rounds out the picture, placing the plays beside the novels and judging how Balzac's crowded, lifelike characters fare in dialogue and action. The volume is short but useful, giving a reader the context to approach plays that rarely reach English stages. It suits Balzac fans curious about his failures and experiments beyond the novels that made his name.
balzac:
Frederick Lawton, an English critic living in Paris, wrote this life of Balzac after Auguste Rodin's statue of the novelist drew him to the subject. Passy saw the dedication dated 1910. Lawton quarrels with critic Brunetiere, who doubted that a writer's life explains the work. For Balzac, Lawton answers, the novels are the life, and the life reads like a novel.

French society after the Revolution, Lawton argues, lay shaken like a town after an earthquake. Balzac rebuilt that broken world in the Comedie Humaine, his linked series of novels. Chapters follow the money troubles, printing schemes, and writing labor behind the books. Taine's praise names Balzac, with Shakespeare and Saint-Simon, a storehouse of knowledge about nature. Lawton inserts notices of the chief novels as their importance demands. Readers who find the shorter Keim life too brief come for a fuller, more critical account of the crowded career.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-antoine-de-la:
Antoine de Lamothe, Sieur de Cadillac, a French soldier born at Toulouse in 1657, became a founder figure in North America. Sent to Acadia in 1683, he studied English colonies, proposed attacks on New York and Boston, and won land on Mount Desert Island. After a troubled return to France, the king sent him back to serve under Frontenac in New France.

As commandant at Michillimackinac from 1694, he managed western native peoples who might join the English. In June 1701 he founded Detroit, building a church and a fort and drawing colonists to the post. Later made governor of Louisiana, he was deposed and jailed in the Bastille, then restored to favour before his death in 1730.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barac:
Barac, Hebrew Baraq, meaning lightning, delivered Israel from the Chanaanites under the judge Debbora. He was the son of Abinoem of Cedes in Nephtali, probably of the tribe of Issachar. After Judge Aod's death, King Jabin of Asor oppressed Israel grievously for twenty years. Debbora, prophetess of Mount Ephraim, urged Barac to muster ten thousand men of Nephtali and Zabulon.

Barac gathered his warriors at Cedes, climbed Mount Thabor, and rushed down to surprise Sisara, Jabin's general. Sisara's panicked army was routed, pursued, and cut to pieces. Sisara himself fled to Jahel, wife of Haber the Cinite, and met a treacherous end in her tent. The victory ended Jabin's power, brought forty years of rest, and lives in Debbora and Barac's triumphal ode.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-count-louis-d:
A biographical entry presents Count Louis de Buade Frontenac, governor of New France, born at Paris in 1622 and dead at Quebec in 1698, godson of Louis XIII. A soldier of brilliant reputation in Europe, he arrived in Canada with honours already won against the Turks at Candia and in the wars of Holland, France, Italy, and Germany.

During his first administration he built Fort Cataracouy, now Kingston, to overawe the Iroquois, and sent La Salle to explore the Mississippi, naming its country Louisiana for Louis XIV. Proud and quarrelsome, he clashed with councillors, the intendant, and Bishop Laval over the liquor trade, and was recalled in 1682. Recalled again in 1689 after the Lachine massacre, he fought Iroquois and English as the colony's deliverer.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-etienne-bonno:
Etienne Bonnot de Condillac was a French philosopher, born at Grenoble on 30 September 1715 and dead near Beaugency on 3 August 1780. He was brother of the Abbé de Mably and himself Abbé of Mureaux. His benefice let him devote himself wholly to study in solitude. About 1755 he became preceptor of the Duke of Parma, writing his Cours d'études for him.

The prince's education completed, Condillac was elected in 1768 to succeed the Abbé d'Olivet in the French Academy. He attended but once, on the day of his reception, then retired to his estate of Flux near Beaugency for the rest of his days. His life falls into two periods. During the first he developed Locke's theories. He published in 1746 his Essai sur l'origine des connaissances humaines, and in 1749 his Traité des systemes, attacking the innate ideas of Descartes, Malebranche, Leibniz, Spinoza, and Boursier.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-francois-hede:
Francois Hedelin, Abbe d'Aubignac, was a French grammarian, poet, preacher, and philologist born at Paris on 4 August 1604 and dead at Nemours on 27 July 1676. He took his name from an abbey granted to him. After classical and theological studies Cardinal Richelieu made him tutor to the cardinal's nephew, the young Duc de Fronsac, whose gratitude brought him a pension of four thousand livres. That post, with his own bent, turned him to literary study, above all the classics.

 The drama drew him most: he wrote a tragedy, Zenobie, and a Practice of the Theatre. Modern scholars prize him chiefly for the Homeric Question, doubting Homer's existence and arguing that the Iliad joins independent ballads gathered by a compiler near Homer's supposed age. Later the ballads were divided again by rhapsodists and finally edited by Pisistratus, views Wolf later echoed with scant credit.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-georges-d-arm:
Georges d'Armagnac, a French cardinal and diplomat born about 1501, served Francis I and the Church through the Wars of Religion. Of the illustrious Foix d'Armagnac house and protégé of Cardinal d'Amboise, he was introduced to Francis I by the Duke of Alençon and named Bishop of Rodez in 1529. He served as ambassador to Venice from 1536 to 1538, fought Charles V, and helped force the emperor's retreat from southern France.

Sent as ambassador to Rome in 1539, d'Armagnac received the cardinal's hat in 1544. He became the king's lieutenant-general at Toulouse in 1552 and archbishop there in 1560. As legate at Avignon from 1565 he defended Church interests against Huguenots and reconciled Avignon with Orange and Languedoc. Pius IV's approval raised him to Avignon's archbishopric in 1576. His learning, austere virtue, and patronage of arts and sciences ranked him first among sixteenth-century servants of the Church.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-isaac:
Abraham and Sarah's son, Isaac stands in Genesis chapters 15 to 35 as the sole legal heir of the chosen people. His name, the entry notes, means “he laughs,” drawn from passages where laughter greets the promise of his birth. Circumcised eight days after birth and weaned in due course, he spent his early years at Beersheba before his father took him to Mount Moriah for sacrifice.

Spared by miracle, he returned home, lost his mother at thirty-six. Later married Rebekah, brought from Mesopotamia by his father's servant to the south country where Isaac lived. Scholars trace the Genesis narrative to three source documents, labeled J, E, and P, and the entry weighs that scholarship against the story's shape. Readers get patriarch, promise, and near-sacrifice in compact form.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacques-marie:
French bishop Jacques Marie Achille Ginoulhiac was born at Montpellier on 3 December 1806. He died there on 17 November 1875. Soon after ordination in 1830, he became professor at Montpellier seminary. Later, in 1839, he became vicar-general at Aix. He was consecrated bishop of Grenoble in 1853. The next year he became assistant to the pontifical throne and knight of the Legion of Honour.

At the Vatican Council he spoke publicly on philosophical errors in December 1869. He spoke on the rule of faith in March and April 1870. He spoke on papal infallibility in May and June 1870. On that point he sided with the minority. He left Rome before the 18 July session that defined the doctrine. In 1870 he moved from Grenoble to the Lyons archbishopric. Fearing Prussian invasion, Lyons' people vowed a basilica at Fourvières if the city were spared. The entry follows a council minority bishop to Lyons.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-melchior-de-p:
Melchior de Polignac, cardinal, diplomat, and writer, was born of an ancient Auvergne family at Le Puy in 1661 and died at Paris in 1742. He studied with distinction at the College de Clermont and the Sorbonne. Still young, he attended the conclave that chose Alexander VIII in 1689 and shared in Rome talks on the Declaration of 1682. In 1691 he witnessed Innocent XII's election, and in 1693 became ambassador extraordinary to Poland.

There he won John Sobieski's favour and secured the Prince de Conti's choice as successor, but Conti's slowness voided the election, and Louis XIV sent Polignac back to his Abbey of Bon-Port. Granted two new abbeys in 1702, he was sent to Rome in 1706, backed France at Gertruydenberg and Utrecht from 1710 to 1713, and became cardinal in 1713. Entangled in Cellamare's conspiracy, he was banished in 1718, then served France at Rome again from 1724 for eight years.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mission-of-sa:
The Mission of San Xavier del Bac was one of eight missions founded by the Spanish padres between 1687 and 1720 in the Pimeria Alta, within present-day Arizona. The others were Guevavi, Tumacacori, Tubac, Sonoita, Arivaca, Santa Ana, and Calabasas. Of the eight, only Tumacacori and San Xavier del Bac survive.

San Xavier, nine miles south of Tucson in the fertile Santa Cruz valley, close to the Papago village, was founded in 1699 by the Jesuit Eusebius Kino. Kino, a Tyrolese, gave up a mathematics chair at Ingolstadt to evangelize the New World. Its church of stone and brick, completed by Spanish Franciscans with one tower unfinished, remains a masterpiece of the desert missions.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-blathmac:
St. Blathmac was a distinguished Irish monk, born in Ireland about 750. He suffered martyrdom in Iona about 835. This entry follows a man fortunate in having his biography written by Strabo, Benedictine abbot of Reichenau from 824 to 849. The story of his martyrdom has thus been handed down through the ages. Strabo's life of the saint, in Latin hexameters, is found in Messingham's Florilegium Insulae Sanctorum, published at Paris in 1624.

A scion of a noble family, Blathmac soon showed a religious turn of mind, longing to join the noble army of martyrs — a wish afterwards fulfilled. His name was Latinized as Florentius, from Irish Blath, meaning a flower. As a religious he was most exemplary, in the end becoming abbot. In 824 he joined the Columban community at Iona, and not long afterwards the Danes ravaged the island, and the entry follows him to his martyrdom at Mass.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-guthlac:
Guthlac, hermit of Croyland, swapped eight years of warfare for fifteen years of fenland penance. Born about 673 of noble Middle Anglian stock, he showed piety as a boy, then spent eight or nine years as a warrior without quite forgetting his early training. Remorse turned him to Repton monastery, where two years of penance fired him to match the desert fathers. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 dates his death at Croyland to 11 April 714.

With two companions he retired to Croyland, a lonely island in Lincolnshire's dismal fens, fasting daily through fifteen rigid years. His life comes from the monk Felix, who dedicated it to King Aethelbald, Guthlac's friend, assuring him every detail came from the saint's old and intimate companions. The entry trusts that chain of witnesses: a soldier's remorse, a fen island, and a hermit's long penance.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stanislaus-du:
Stanislaus du Lac, a Jesuit educationist, ran the school that fed France's great military and scientific academies. Born at Paris on 21 November 1835, he was son of Louis Paul Albert du Lac de Fugères and Camille de Rouvroy de Lamairie. His father's family was noted in history since 1206. He entered the Jesuit novitiate at Issenheim in Alsace on 28 October 1853. He studied theology at Laval until ordained priest on 19 September 1869.

The next summer he became rector of Sainte-Croix College at Le Mans, where during the Franco-Prussian War he organised an efficient hospital service. Twenty-two thousand soldiers sojourned successively in his college during his ten months there. In October 1871 he succeeded the martyred Léon Ducoudray as rector of Sainte-Geneviève, called La Rue des Postes. From 1872 to 1881 his pupils won 213 places at Centrale, 328 at Polytechnique, and 830 at Saint-Cyr. He died at Paris on 30 August 1909.
doe-osti-17011958-machine-learning-assis: Teaching fiber-optic cables to hear microreactors got its DOE report, and this text covers ML-assisted acoustic sensing. The algorithms learn the sounds of a healthy core. Tiny reactors get watchful AI ears. The research was logged. The ears were watchful.
doe-osti-17076694-machine-learning-assis: Microreactor fiber listening got its DOE report again, and this text covers ML-assisted distributed acoustic sensing. The pages record the AI ears. The tiny reactors get their monitors. The sensing was machine-learned. The monitors were tiny. The ears were AI.
doe-osti-2589499-active-power-control-on: Wind turbine power control got its CRADA final, and this report covers active machine control. The pages record the outcomes. The wind operators get their closeout. The control was active power. The machines were wind turbine. The operators got closeouts.
doe-osti-2998227-speed-optimizations-for: Ray trace algorithms got speed-optimized, and this DOE report covers the physics improvements. The pages detail the methods. The graphics folks get their speedup. The algorithms were ray trace. The improvements were physics. The folks were graphics. The speedup was graphics.
doe-osti-2999135-intergraph-cps-a-graph-: InterGraph-CPS got its graph theory, and this DOE report characterizes cyber-physical links. The pages detail the interdependency work. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BusinessExecuti:
Business Executives Move for Vietnam Peace organized the wing of the antiwar movement that wore suits. This file holds the program and contents of its first national meeting, held September 27, 1967, at the Statler Hilton Hotel in Washington.

The meeting's remarks included those of its co-chairman, Senator Thruston B. Morton of Kentucky, a Republican breaking with the war policy of the Johnson years. Programs fix who spoke, in what order, and under what banners, which makes them useful records of a movement's public face. This one documents the moment opposition to the war reached the boardroom.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-SmithSegioArcac: An FBI memorandum dated March 6, 1967, sent from Papich to Brennan, records information supplied by a liaison agent. The file is cataloged under the name Sergio Arcacha Smith. It is a single internal bureau memo, the kind written to pass one office's report to another. Readers tracing how the FBI handled outside sources in the late 1960s can see that routine in the bureau's own words.
honore-de-balzac:
Albert Keim and Louis Lumet, two French men of letters, wrote this biography of Honore de Balzac, the novelist behind the Human Comedy. Frederic Taber Cooper translated their French text into English for American readers. Balzac (1799-1850) wrote at furious speed, in debt for most of his adult life. Keim and Lumet present his career as a triumph of will over chaos.

Nine chapters run from a boyhood treatise on the human will to the garret where young Balzac starved and wrote. Business failures, printing losses, and dandy dress show a man spending ahead of his earnings. First success, the Foreign Lady who became his wife, and the house at Les Jardies carry the middle years. Victor Hugo's graveside praise opens the book and sets its admiring tone. Readers new to Balzac get a fast, warm life story before tackling the novels themselves.
kelly-miller-an-appeal-to-conscience-ame:
Kelly Miller wrote this protest against America's caste code, published by Macmillan in 1920 with an introduction by Albert Bushnell Hart. Miller was dean of the College of Arts and Sciences at Howard University in Washington. Miller argues that the nation judges Black citizens by one standard and white citizens by another, and that this habit shames its claim to democracy. The introduction praises the book's calm temper while summing up that charge.

Five chapters carry the case: Race Contact, Lawlessness, Segregation, Negro Patriotism and Devotion, and Righteousness. Miller attacks lynching and the Jim Crow laws, defends Black loyalty in war, and insists that fair dealing is a moral duty owed to every citizen. The book closes as it opens, as an appeal to the conscience of right-minded America.
monarch-the-big-bear-of-tallac:
Ernest Thompson Seton published this animal biography in 1919, with a hundred drawings of his own. He heard the tale by a fire in the pines of Mount Tallac, in the Sierra Nevada. Two rough hunters told it in broken bits, a sentence at a time. Seton says their gestures and snarls told as much as their words.

Their subject was Monarch, a giant grizzly of the Tallac country. Seton reads the bear's life as a parable of hill-born power. Like the redwood, the avalanche, and the river, such power grows on the peaks and fades on the plains. His nature writing mixes tracking lore with open sympathy for wild animals.
monsieur-de-pourceaugnac:
Molière's farce Monsieur de Pourceaugnac was acted on October 6, 1669. Charles Heron Wall translated it into English prose, with introductions and notes. The introduction calls it nothing but a farce, and one of the best of its kind. Molière himself acted the title part.

A pompous provincial comes to Paris to marry Julia, whose lover Éraste wants her himself. The Neapolitan adventurer Sbrigani organizes the torment. Two physicians and an apothecary attack the visitor with the era's medicine, which Molière mocks savagely. Disguises, false wives, and police officers complete the machinery of this boisterous comedy of vanity.
nasa-tm-19680004505-flight-evaluation-of:
Daniel J. Lesco, at the Lewis Research Center in Cleveland, wrote this memorandum in January 1968. Numbered TM X-1488, it gives a flight evaluation of an electrostatic accelerometer. The instrument measures the very low-level accelerations a spacecraft feels in orbit, such as the gentle push of venting gas. Ordinary accelerometers cannot sense such pushes cleanly.

Conventional instruments suffer a null bias, a false output at zero input, as large as the tiny accelerations themselves. The miniature electrostatic design suspends its proof mass electrically, which removes that bias problem. On its first flight test, aboard an orbiting Saturn S-IVB stage on the AS-203 mission, it measured liquid hydrogen venting accelerations at tiny levels. They sat far below a thousandth of Earth's gravity. Lesco compares the readings with other flight measurements and correlates the output with firings of the attitude control system.
nasa-tm-19680018145-synthesis-of-organic:
C. Ponnamperuma and co-authors F. Woeller, J. Flores, M. Ramirez, and W. Allen of Ames Research Center test how organic compounds form under electric discharges in this study. The work simulates the primitive Earth's atmosphere, thought to hold mainly methane, ammonia, and water. Such experiments probe how life's building blocks could arise without life.

Energy sources on the early Earth included sunlight, heat, ionizing radiation, and lightning-like discharges. Discharges act close to the surface, so their products could reach early oceans effectively. The team ran discharge experiments to mimic those prebiotic reactions. Their paper describes attempts to form organic substances by this route. The results bear on chemical evolution before biology began.
nasa-tm-19680024922-optimal-control-of-s:
William P. Kavanaugh, Elwood C. Stewart, and David H. Brocker of Ames Research Center apply random search to satellite attitude control in this 1968 conference paper. Some control problems amount to finding the lowest point of a performance surface. That surface is often unknown, discontinuous, and full of peaks, valleys, and flat regions.

Random search suits such rough surfaces well. The authors review an adaptive random search algorithm from their earlier work. That algorithm had hunted the minimum of a boundary surface from optimal control theory. Here they apply it to satellite attitude acquisition, the task of pointing a satellite correctly. A hybrid computer ran the search described in the paper.
nasa-tm-19710015775-long-term-drift-of-s:
G E Glawe and A J Szaniszlo of the Lewis Research Center wrote this paper for a June 1971 temperature meeting in Washington. It reports how heat sensors called thermocouples drift over very long use. The test pairs used noble and refractory metals with pure alumina insulation. Runs lasted up to ten thousand hours at extreme heat.

Thirty eight pairs aged in air, argon, and vacuum. In air, the best platinum pairs drifted only a few degrees over the full run. In argon, drift grew larger, and thin wires behaved erratically. In one vacuum rig, most noble metal pairs failed within a few thousand hours. The team checked chemical and physical changes behind the drift.
nasa-tm-19720007141-flight-investigation:
Verlon L Head of the Lewis Research Center reported these nozzle flights in January 1972, as NASA TM X-2478. A modified F-106B jet carried engine nacelles under its wings. Three variable flap ejector nozzles were flown in that mounting. Tunnel tests alone cannot show how a wing and fuselage change nozzle behavior. These flights measured the real installed case.

Crews gathered nozzle thrust values during the flights. They also measured boattail drag, the drag on the nacelle's tapered rear. Boundary layer readings near the nozzles completed the data set. Designers could then compare mounted and isolated nozzle performance directly. The work continued a long Lewis program on ejector nozzles for advanced jets.
nasa-tm-19720011982-flight-test-of-carbo:
Thomas E Walton Jr and William G Witte of the Langley Research Center reported this heat shield flight test in March 1972, as NASA TM X-2504. A recoverable spacecraft rode the Pacemaker vehicle system. Its shield was carbon phenolic, half carbon fiber and half phenolic resin. Fiber direction varied across different areas of the shield. The flight pushed heating on the round nose to extreme rates.

The nose suffered the greatest mass loss in the test. High heating rates and likely flaking of char shared the blame. The cone section behind wore down evenly, with uniform char depth. Heating measurements suggested the boundary layer had turned turbulent. Sound sensors in the layer gave a new kind of transition evidence. That sensing idea interested the authors for future free flight studies.
parkman-count-frontenac:
Francis Parkman published Count Frontenac and New France under Louis XIV in 1877. The book forms Part Five of his France and England in North America. Frontenac, the great governor, returns for his second term in Canada.

King William's War burns along the frontier as the volume opens. Frontenac defends Quebec and strikes back with raids of his own. Parkman paints the old lion of New France in bold, bright strokes. Court plots in Paris cross with war in the snowy woods. Many readers call this the most dramatic volume of the whole long series. Frontenac himself dominates it like a figure from epic.
podcast-dannyjones-Mrdv2rwqrAc:
Interviewer Brandon Bowen asks fans and members about the metal band GWAR for Danny Jones. GWAR plays in monster costumes with fake blood and wild stage acts. The segment asks if anyone still listens.

Fans call the band pure chaos and total entertainment. One compares them to a metal version of shock acts before them. Bowen collects short, funny replies on what the music means to each person. The piece is brief and playful. It works as a snapshot of a cult band's hold on fans who love theater as much as riffs.
podcast-joerogan-0pmviUS1Zac:
Astrophysicist Neil deGrasse Tyson joins Joe Rogan for episode 1347 of the Joe Rogan Experience. Tyson is the best known face of space science on US TV. His talks mix hard facts with jokes and a teacher's flair.

Tyson and Rogan roam the cosmos, from black holes to the odds of life on far worlds. Tyson bats down fringe claims with a grin and a fact. Rogan asks the big kid questions his crowd loves. Listeners get a fun, dense tour of the sky. The library keeps the episode as a record of a famed guest at ease.
podcast-tuckercarlson-S3aYb4j6XAc:
Former CIA officer John Kiriakou briefs Tucker Carlson on Iran, false flags, and what is really happening in Washington. Kiriakou, the whistleblower who exposed the agency's torture program, gives a spy's warning here. His latest briefing questions the stories the public is being told.

Kiriakou gives his truth about the standoff with Iran and the risk of a staged trigger for war. He explains how false flag claims should be judged by someone who worked inside. Carlson asks what officials are hiding from the president himself. Skeptical and watchful viewers are told to listen well.
the-chateau-of-prince-polignac:
A tale from the 1864 Chapman and Hall gathering Tales of All Countries opens with a town few English readers know: Le Puy, capital of the old province of Le Velay. The district now goes by the imperial name of the Department of the Haute Loire. It lies southeast of Auvergne, near the center of the southern half of France.

The telling lingers on the town's strange volcanic ground. Hard rocks rise sheer from a narrow valley, the town clusters round two of them, and a third stands a mile off. The highest, the Rocher de Corneille, once held a castle on its summit. There a great bronze figure of the Virgin, cast from cannon taken at Sebastopol, was to stand. Halfway down stands the cathedral, a gloomy Romanesque pile built out on huge supports, reached by a striking flight of steps. Place itself is the tale's first character.
the-fighting-governor-a-chronicle-of-fro:
Charles W. Colby wrote The Fighting Governor as a tale of Frontenac and old Canada, volume seven of the Chronicles of Canada, printed at Toronto in 1915. The first chapter paints the Canada of 1672.

Colby says the colony Frontenac came to rule held fewer than seven thousand souls, yet ran on forms as strict as those of France. He traces that rule back through French kings to the days of St. Louis and the wars of nobles. Divine right ruled at Paris and at Quebec alike. Frontenac's clashes with priests and traders grow from that tight frame of crown power.
the-love-affairs-of-a-bibliomaniac:
Eugene Field's The Love Affairs of a Bibliomaniac was introduced by his brother, who explains that the sketches grew from a lifetime of book-hunting. Field spent nearly a quarter century in journalism celebrating the pleasures of collecting. His library, the introduction says, was as valuable as it was interesting, bought at great personal sacrifice by a comparatively poor man.

Field called bibliomania a disease and a soothing affliction, and mocked fellow collectors in his newspaper column while chasing musty prizes himself. The introduction quotes his Bibliomaniac's Prayer, asking that his temptation be a book, purchased and kept, at which other men would wail to learn how cheaply he got it. Readers meet a collector who laughs at his own incurable habit.
the-story-of-little-black-sambo-and-the-:
Helen Bannerman's two picture stories are paired in one volume. Her preface explains their origin. An English lady in India invented tales for her two little girls. She drew and coloured the pictures herself. Sambo's tale was invented during a long railway journey. It was the favourite. It went into a Dumpy Book. Bannerman hoped other children would like it as much.

The story gives Sambo a red coat and blue trousers made by his mother, Black Mumbo, and a green umbrella and purple shoes bought at the bazaar by his father, Black Jumbo. Grand in his fine clothes, he walks into the jungle, where a tiger demands the coat as the price of not eating him, and further tigers follow.
women-in-the-life-of-balzac: Juanita H. Floyd wrote this study of women in the life of French novelist Honore de Balzac. Pages present here hold only a publisher's header giving the title and her name, plus long donation appeals. No title page, chapter list, or study text appears in these pages. The header alone cannot show which women Floyd treats or what she argues about their place in Balzac's life and fiction.
